name: Parthenon

facts.label: of Ionic frieze round the cella

modelNote: Footprint fitted to OpenStreetMap; stylobate, columns, entablature and pediments from published dimensions; the ruin after 1687 and the restorations read on photos. The interior, the roofs, the statue and the later additions are interpreted from descriptions.

evidence.identity: Parthenon (Παρθενών), Acropolis of Athens, Athens, Greece (OpenStreetMap way 910010406)

sources.read: Stylobate 69.5 × 30.9 m, height 13.72 m, 8 × 17 columns, 92 metopes (14/14/32/32); Older Parthenon begun after Marathon and destroyed in 480 BC; built from 447 BC, Athena Parthenos dedicated in 439/438 BC; 3rd-century fire and 4th-century roof of clay tiles over the cella alone, steeper, wings exposed; church with an apse where the pronaos was; Latin tower at the south-west corner; mosque with minaret; 26 September 1687 explosion: six columns south, eight north and the pronaos except one fell, about 300 dead; smaller mosque in the ruin; Elgin 1801–1812; minaret pulled down to its base and stair after 1832; 1839 photograph; ESMA 1975; crane folding under the roofline; west scaffolding removed September 2025; restored west pediment unveiled June 2026.

Stylobate 30.86 × 69.51 m on a three-step krepis; columns 1.90 m across and 10.43 m high, corner columns 4.3 cm thicker, 10–12 drums, 20 flutes; corner contraction about 61.5 cm; entablature 3.29 m; pediment 28.35 m wide, 3.46 m high, 0.91 m deep; naos 29.80 × 19.20 m, door 4.92 m wide and 10 m high, nave 10.60 m clear; two-storey interior Doric colonnade on three sides; porches of six columns; west room 13.36 m deep with four Ionic columns; curvature 60 mm on the short and 110 mm on the long sides; columns leaning 7.4 cm inwards; Athena about 11 m on a base of 4.09 × 8.04 m.

Acropolis Restoration Service leaflet: Doric peripteral temple, 8 by 17 columns with an inner row of 6 at each end; two-storey interior colonnades; built 447–438 BC by Iktinos and Kallikrates under Phidias; 160 m Ionic frieze; 13 m statue; pediment subjects; 6th-century church with an apse at the east and the entrance moved west; 12th-century repairs and a staircase in the opisthonaos; Catholic church then mosque with a minaret; 1687 explosion; Pittakis from 1842; Balanos 1894–1933 with iron and cement, misplaced members; ESMA from 1975, worksite from 1983; east side to 1991; south column 1993; west frieze removed 1993; north colonnade: 230 members, 900 t, cement drums replaced with Pentelic marble, finished 2010; pronaos 1995–2004, flutes of the supplements still to carve; the rotating crane in the cella.

Completed interventions: east side 1984–1991; south colonnade 5th column from the east 1992–1993, lifted from the second drum up in one piece; pronaos 1995–2004 (columns 4 and 5 fully restored, 1–3 partly, the 6th from the north reassembled); opisthonaos 1992–2004; north colonnade from October 2001, columns 4th to 11th from the east, flutes carved 2011–2014; west side 2011–2015; derrick crane in the cella from 1983 and Potain crane from 2002.

Older Parthenon begun after Marathon (c. 490–88 BC) on a massive limestone foundation, still under construction when the Persians destroyed it in 480 BC; left in ruin 33 years; Hill’s stylobate 23.51 × 66.888 m; platform smaller and slightly north of the final Parthenon; three steps (two of poros, one of Karrha limestone); its column drums built into the north curtain wall.

After Korres: the Older Parthenon was the first Doric temple built entirely of marble, the Pentelikon quarries being opened for it; columns c. 1.90 m across; work had reached the second or third column drums when it was halted.

NOVA on the restoration: about 70,000 pieces; Balanos set members in the wrong places and used iron clamps without the lead sheathing, which rusted and cracked the marble; pairs of cedar pieces centred the drums like a key in a lock and still smelled of cedar; new marble from Pentelicon; titanium pairs for the restoration.

Greek cranes from the late 6th century BC, known from cuttings for lifting tongs and lewis irons on temple blocks; a winch and pulley system that replaced ramps; blocks under 15–20 t; treadwheel cranes are Roman.

Conversion to a mosque after 1458, 1466–70 more likely; the Frankish tower converted into a minaret; the apse mosaic survived; destroyed in 1687; a smaller free-standing single-domed mosque in the cleared naos in the early 18th century, removed in 1843.

Consecrated in 438 BC; about 11.50 m probably with its base; poros pedestal 8.065 × 4.10 m; gold 40–50 talents on a cypress frame, ivory face and arms; eastern room 29.90 × 19 m, ceiling about 12.50 m; water basin in front; after the late-antique fire the naos’ Doric columns were replaced with columns from Hellenistic stoas; lost at an unknown date, not mentioned once the temple became a church.

A colonnade of 23 smaller Doric columns in two storeys round the statue; west room with four Ionic columns; widths 30.875/30.8835 m and lengths 69.5151/69.5115 m; about 13,400 stones; 1180: central entablature section removed to enlarge the apse; 1205 Latin church; 1458 mosque.

Peripteral Doric temple of 8 by 17 columns, built 447–438 BC by Ictinus and Callicrates; a double-tiered Doric colonnade in a Π inside; four Ionic columns in the west room; roof of marble tiles with anthemia and lion-head gutters, statues as akroteria at the corners.

Evan Hadingham (Smithsonian, 2008), reprinted: 100,000 t of marble from a quarry 11 miles from Athens; ropes, pulleys and wooden cranes; iron clamps in carved grooves sealed with molten lead; flutes carved after erection, as costly as quarrying, hauling and setting together; built in eight or nine years; the restoration’s collapsible crane in the cella, scaffolding of steel poles, about 70 craftsmen from Tinos, titanium clamps and rods, soluble white cement; Korres’ collar lifting the 55-tonne column.

references.camera: About 100 m east of the temple’s centre (Commons camera location), on the rock: the east front, the middle of its pediment missing, the restored pronaos behind.
About 85 m west of the centre (Commons camera location), coming up from the Propylaea: the west front after its scaffolding came down, the Erechtheion on the left.
At the north-east corner (Commons camera location), wide angle: the east front receding left, the north colonnade with its new marble drums receding right.
Below the south colonnade (Commons camera location), wide angle looking up: the west group of columns, the stumps of 1687 and the east group beyond.
About 650 m south-east, from Makrygianni (Commons camera location), with a long lens: the south flank with its gap of 1687 and the east front; the west end in scaffolding (May 2015).

features.text: A Doric peripteral temple of 8 by 17 columns, 46 in all, with an inner row of six columns at each end.
Columns 10.43 m high and 1.90 m across, in 10–12 drums with 20 flutes; corner columns 4.3 cm thicker and the corner bays closed up by 61.5 cm.
An entablature 3.29 m high with 92 metopes between triglyphs: 14 on each front, 32 on each flank.
Pediments 28.35 m wide, 3.46 m high and 0.91 m deep, under raking cornices.
No straight lines: the stylobate rises 60 mm on the short sides and 110 mm on the long ones; the columns lean 7.4 cm inwards.
A roof of marble tiles with antefixes (anthemia) and lion-head spouts.
A continuous Ionic frieze 160 m long round the top of the cella, over the porches.
Inside, a two-storey Doric colonnade in a Π round the statue; a back room with four Ionic columns.
Close details: cedar centring pieces between drums, iron clamps sealed in lead.
Today the north colonnade stands complete with new white marble among the ancient drums, the south side has its gap of 1687, and the middle of the east pediment is gone.

evidence.geometry: The outline of the lowest step (OpenStreetMap) gives the place and orientation (12.9° north of east); stylobate, columns, intercolumniation, entablature, pediment and curvature from de.wikipedia; step heights and the state of the ruin read on four Commons photos fitted with calibrate.mjs.

gaps: Ref 0 (east): columns, entablature and the two surviving ends of the pediment lie within a few pixels of the photo; the south end of the pediment runs a little further towards the middle in the photo.
Ref 1 (west): the facade fits, but the model’s pediment apex stood about 0.4 m above the photo’s: the raking sima is lost at the apex today, and the apex point had been read on the sima.
Ref 2 (north-east): columns and capitals fit; on the photo the north flank keeps its cornice only at the corners, with bare frieze blocks between, where the model had a continuous cornice.

Ref 3 (south): the model laid a continuous entablature over the gap of 1687 (elements that named only the north flank laid the other sides whole), and its column stumps in the gap stood lower than on the photo; the south cornice is also missing between the corners.
Everywhere: the model’s marble reads greyer and more even than the warm, patched stone of the photos, and the metopes and pediment figures were plain blocks.

Full pass (5 references, 15 phases): ref 4, the 650 m telephoto from the south-east, was captured at the viewer’s default lens, the temple a speck: the viewer then ignored fields of view of 10° or less.
The east metope reliefs read almost black: on the morning photo the top of each panel lies in the shadow of the cornice.
On ref 2 the north flank still has a few cornice blocks between the corners; the model keeps the cornice only within 3 m of them.
In the ancient worksites the gin poles stood beside the scaffold with their foot in the air, following the height of the work.
fixed: The entablature brick now lays only the sides an element names: the gap of 1687 on the south flank is open, and the fronts are no longer laid twice.
The flanks’ cornice is kept only within 3 m of the corners, as on the photos (its loss shown in 1687, an interpreted date).
The stumps of the 6th to 9th south columns raised to 9, 5, 8 and 10 drums, read on the south-east telephoto of 2015 and the south photos.
The west apex point refitted on the raking geison (the sima lost); the tympanum’s courses carried up under the raking cornice so no step shows.
The 28 metopes of the two fronts and three pediment groups laid as photo reliefs from the October 2025 photos (CC BY-SA 4.0, AleWi).
A fifth reference added, from the south-east (2015), so that the views cover three sides.
The east metopes are laid on their sunlit lower 0.8 m only; the shaded top stays plain stone.
The ancient gin poles stand on the ground, tall enough to reach the entablature (17 m) and the pediment (21 m).
The viewer now takes fields of view down to 1° (kit change by the studio session, c5f86ed): ref 4 is captured with its fitted 5.5° lens from its real place.

gaps: Ref 0 (east) and ref 1 (west): columns, entablature, pediments and the photo-relief metopes lie on the photos; the photos show patched stone (new white marble in the west tympanum, weathered orange on the west columns) where the model’s marble is one even honey colour.
Ref 1 (west): the photo’s raking cornices are broken and have lost their sima; the model shows them whole.
Ref 2 (north-east): the colonnade fits drum for drum; on the photo a few cornice blocks still stand on the north flank between the corners, the model has none there.
Ref 3 (south): the west group, the four broken columns and the east group fit; the photo’s scaffolding and crane of 2020 are gone from the final state.

Ref 4 (south-east, 2015): the columns, the gap and the east front fit the telephoto; below them the model shows its krepis where the photo shows the Acropolis’s south wall in front, and the modern crane stands elsewhere than the kit’s crane model.
remaining: The rock of the Acropolis, its walls and its other monuments are not modelled (studio).
The flanks’ cornice is kept only at the corners; a few blocks survive between them on the north side.
The raking simas are shown complete.
The marble is one colour; new marble shows drum by drum only, not as patches.
Interior, roofs, statue, apse, tower, minaret and small mosque are interpreted reconstructions.
Only the 28 metopes of the fronts and three pediment groups are photo reliefs; the frieze and the other metopes are plain.

uncertainties: The earlier temple’s place on the platform is not known: it is centred on the later axis and set 1.5 m north.
The porches’ columns, the cella walls’ thickness, the interior colonnade’s spacing, the west room’s columns and the ceilings are interpreted from Doric proportions and descriptions.

Wikipedia counts six columns fallen on the south side in 1687; the photos of 2020–2022 show five gaps, three of them with columns standing to part height. The model follows the photos (the 6th to 10th from the east).
The share and places of cement drums (Balanos) and new marble drums (restoration) are interpreted.
Athena Parthenos is a simplified figure: only her size, materials and attributes are documented.
The 4th-century roof’s pitch, the apse, the tower’s top, the minaret and the small mosque are sized by interpretation.

The acroteria and the pediment and metope sculpture are not modelled in stone; scaffolds and hoists of the ancient worksites are reconstructions (the sources speak of wooden cranes, ropes and pulleys).

The 28 metopes of the east and west fronts and three pediment groups are photo reliefs of the carving as it is in October 2025 (copies since 1984–1991 on the east and 2011–2015 on the west, YSMA, or weathered originals), laid on every state since 438 BC; the other metopes and the frieze are plain stone.
The raking simas, mostly lost today, are shown complete.
The crane of the modern worksite is shown with the kit’s metal crane model, standing in for the derrick (1983) and Potain (2002) cranes in the cella.
The rock of the Acropolis and its walls are not modelled: seen from below the south wall (ref 4) or from the Propylaea they hide the krepis in the photos.
The north flank keeps a few cornice blocks between the corners; the model keeps the cornice only within 3 m of them.
The marble is shown in one honey colour; the photos show new white marble patched into ancient blocks, which the model renders drum by drum only.

phases.title: The older Parthenon
phases.text: After Marathon a massive limestone platform levels the south of the Acropolis, and a marble temple is begun on it. Work stops when its columns stand two or three drums high.

moments.title: The first temple all of marble
moments.text: It was the first Doric temple built entirely of marble: the quarries of Mount Pentelikon were opened for it.

phases.title: Burnt by the Persians
phases.text: The Persians sack Athens and the unfinished temple burns. The site is left in ruin for 33 years.

moments.title: Drums in the city wall
moments.text: The burnt column drums were built into the curtain wall north of the Acropolis, where they can still be seen.

phases.title: Pericles’ temple
phases.text: Iktinos and Kallikrates raise a Doric temple of 8 by 17 columns in Pentelic marble, under Phidias’ supervision. In 438 BC his gold and ivory Athena is dedicated inside.

moments.title: Cedar at the heart of each drum
moments.text: Two pieces of cedar, fitted one inside the other like a key in a lock, centred each drum on the one below. Opened 2,500 years later, they still smelled of cedar.

moments.title: Not one straight line
moments.text: The stylobate rises 11 cm towards the middle of the long sides and 6 cm on the short ones; the columns lean 7.4 cm inwards.

moments.title: Iron in lead
moments.text: The blocks were tied with iron clamps set in carved grooves, then molten lead was poured over them against corrosion and earthquakes.

moments.title: Flutes carved last
moments.text: The flutes were cut on the standing columns, and carving them probably cost as much as all the quarrying, hauling and setting together.

moments.title: A goddess of gold and ivory
moments.text: Athena Parthenos stood about 11.5 m high with her pedestal, clad in some 40 to 50 talents of gold over a cypress frame, before a basin of water.

phases.title: The pediments
phases.text: Statues fill the pediments: the Birth of Athena on the east, her contest with Poseidon on the west. With the 92 metopes and the 160 m frieze, no temple had carried so much sculpture.

moments.title: Two stories on two fronts
moments.text: The east pediment shows the Birth of Athena, the west her contest with Poseidon for Athens; the metopes the Gigantomachy, Troy, Amazons and Centaurs.

phases.title: Fire and a steeper roof
phases.text: A fire after the middle of the 3rd century destroys the roof and much of the interior. The repairs give the cella alone a new timber roof with clay tiles, steeper than the first.

moments.title: Columns from the agora
moments.text: The burnt Doric columns of the naos were replaced with columns taken from Hellenistic stoas in the Roman agora.

phases.title: The church of the Virgin
phases.text: The temple becomes a church: an apse for the Holy Bema is built at the east end and the entrance is moved to the west.

moments.title: Where did Athena go?
moments.text: The statue is never mentioned once the temple was a church: whether it was destroyed or carried off is unknown.

phases.title: Panaghia Atheniotissa
phases.text: The church is a place of pilgrimage. It is repaired in the 12th century and a staircase is added in the back porch.

moments.title: A hole in the pediment
moments.text: In 1180 the middle of the east front’s upper works was taken down to enlarge the apse, by ancient-greece.org’s account.

phases.title: A Latin cathedral
phases.text: Under the Franks the Parthenon becomes a Roman Catholic church. A tower is added at its south-west corner.

moments.title: A tower in the porch
moments.text: The tower at the south-west corner may have been a bell tower; its base and spiral stair still rise to the architrave.

phases.title: A mosque
phases.text: After the Ottoman conquest the church becomes a mosque, probably around 1466–70. The tower is raised into a minaret and the apse serves as the mihrab.

moments.title: A mosque in a temple
moments.text: The Frankish tower was raised into a minaret; the Virgin’s mosaic in the apse evidently survived the conversion.

phases.title: The explosion
phases.text: During the Venetian siege a mortar shell hits the gunpowder the Ottomans had stored inside. The middle of the temple is blown out and about 300 people die.

moments.title: Fourteen columns down
moments.text: Six columns fell on the south side, eight on the north, and the front porch except one column; the cella walls crumbled.

phases.title: A mosque in the ruin
phases.text: A small single-domed mosque is built in the cleared space of the naos. Between 1801 and 1812 Elgin’s agents take about half the surviving sculptures to Britain.

moments.title: The Elgin marbles
moments.text: Agents of the Earl of Elgin removed about half the surviving sculptures between 1801 and 1812; the legality of the permission he claimed is disputed.

moments.title: Bullets from the clamps
moments.text: Besieged in 1821–22, the Ottoman garrison tried to melt the lead round the columns’ clamps to cast bullets.

phases.title: The archaeological site
phases.text: Free Greece clears the Acropolis of its later buildings: the minaret is pulled down to its base and the little mosque removed in 1843. K. Pittakis consolidates the cella’s north wall.

moments.title: The first photograph
moments.text: Joly de Lotbinière’s view of 1839, published in 1842, is the first photograph of the Acropolis, and the only image of the mosque in the cella.

phases.title: Balanos’ restoration
phases.text: After the earthquake of 1894 N. Balanos consolidates and restores the temple, and in 1923–33 sets the north colonnade back up. He uses iron and cement, and puts members in the wrong places.

moments.title: Rust in the marble
moments.text: The ancient iron was sheathed in lead; Balanos’ clamps were not, and as they rusted they swelled and split the marble.

phases.title: The great restoration
phases.text: The Committee for the Conservation of the Acropolis Monuments, founded in 1975, opens its worksite in 1983. Thousands of members are taken down, repaired with titanium and new Pentelic marble, and set back where they belong.

moments.title: A 55-tonne column lifted
moments.text: In 1992–93 the leaning 5th column from the east on the south side was lifted from its second drum up in one piece, so that its foot could be repaired.

moments.title: 900 tonnes of the north side
moments.text: In the north colonnade 230 members weighing 900 tonnes were dismantled, freed of rusting iron and set back in their true places; Balanos’ cement drums became new marble.

moments.title: Titanium
moments.text: The new clamps and rods are titanium, which cannot rust and split the stone, and the repairs are set in soluble white cement so they can be undone.

phases.title: Without scaffolding
phases.text: The scaffolding that had encased the temple for decades comes down from the west front in September 2025. The restored west pediment is unveiled in June 2026.

moments.title: The west pediment
moments.text: The restored west pediment was unveiled in June 2026, after the west front’s scaffolding came down in September 2025.

elements.note: The earlier temple’s three steps, sized on Hill’s stylobate of 23.51 × 66.888 m; its exact place on the platform is unknown (Wikipedia: smaller and slightly to the north), so it is centred on the later axis and set 1.5 m north.

6 × 16 columns of c. 1.90 m standing two drums high, the height work had reached when it stopped (archaeology.wiki, after Korres); unfluted, as drums were set before fluting. Spacing even, places interpreted.
Stylobate 69.51 × 30.86 m on three steps, fitted to the OpenStreetMap outline of the lowest step; step heights read on the photos.
Columns 10.43 m high, 1.90 m across (corners 1.943 m), 20 flutes, axes 4.296 m apart with the corners closed up by 61.5 cm, leaning 7.4 cm inwards.
The lower drums of the south columns that still stand to part height in the gap left in 1687, as the 2020–2022 photos show them.
The columns thrown down in 1687: eight on the north (the 4th to 11th from the east, those dismantled and reset in 2001–2010) and the south gap read on the photos.
Balanos’s re-erection of the north colonnade in 1923–33, with cement drums among the ancient ones; which drums were cement is interpreted.
The north colonnade reset in 2001–2010, its cement drums replaced by new Pentelic marble (YSMA); the share and places of the new drums are interpreted from the photos.
Prostyle porches of six columns (YSMA); their diameter (1.71 m), height and spacing are interpreted from Doric proportions and the photos.
The front porch fell in 1687 except one column, the 6th from the north (Wikipedia, YSMA).
The pronaos restored in 1995–2004: two columns in full, three in part, the flutes of their new marble not yet carved (YSMA); the partial heights are interpreted.
The fronts’ entablature, 3.29 m high: architrave, frieze of triglyphs and 14 metopes, geison with mutules.
The flanks’ architrave and frieze of triglyphs and 32 metopes, where their columns stand.
The flanks’ cornice where it survives, at the corners, as on the photos.

The entablature carried by the columns that fell in 1687.
The north entablature set back by Balanos (1923–33), dismantled in 2001 (YSMA).

Pediment 28.35 m wide, 3.46 m high and 0.91 m deep (de.wikipedia), with raking geison and sima.
The east pediment’s ends, which still stand.
The middle of the east pediment, missing today; its removal is dated 1180 by ancient-greece.org, and its width is read on the east photo.
Marble pan and cover tiles with antefixes along the eaves (visitgreece.gr); tile size and the timber frame under them are interpreted.
The marble ceilings of the pterons, beams and coffered slabs, simplified.
The west pteron’s marble ceiling, simplified; parts of it still stand.
The cella’s walls that still stand: the west wall with its door and the west ends of the side walls, stepping down eastwards as on the photos; course heights interpreted.
The cella walls brought down in 1687; the naos is 29.8 × 19.2 m inside and its door 4.92 m wide and 10 m high (de.wikipedia), the wall thickness is interpreted.
The back porch’s architrave with its regulae and the Ionic frieze running on round the cella (YSMA: 160 m).
The front porch’s architrave and frieze, fallen with its columns in 1687.
A two-storey Doric colonnade on three sides of the naos, 23 columns (ancient-greece.org) in a Π (visitgreece.gr); spacing and sizes interpreted, central nave 10.6 m clear (de.wikipedia).
After the late-antique fire the naos columns were replaced with columns from Hellenistic stoas (Wikipedia, Athena Parthenos); shown plain, interpreted.
The west room, 13.36 m deep (de.wikipedia), with four Ionic columns (visitgreece.gr); their places and size interpreted.
A timber ceiling about 12.5 m above the naos floor (Wikipedia, Athena Parthenos); its beams interpreted.

Athena Parthenos simplified: her pedestal 8.065 × 4.10 m, about 11.5 m with it, gold and ivory, the Victory on her right hand, shield and spear, a basin of water in front (Wikipedia). Lost at an unknown date; not mentioned once the temple was a church.
The 4th-century roof of clay tiles over the cella alone, steeper than the first and leaving the wings open (Wikipedia); its pitch is interpreted.
The apse of the Holy Bema built at the east end in the 6th century (YSMA); its size and windows are interpreted.
The tower at the south-west corner (Wikipedia); its base and spiral stair still stand to the architrave. Its plan size is interpreted.
The top of the Latin tower, perhaps a bell tower (Wikipedia, Parthenon mosque); its form is interpreted.

The small single-domed mosque built in the naos in the early 18th century and removed in 1843 (Wikipedia, Parthenon mosque); its size and openings are interpreted.
